questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the arrangement that outlasts the generations inheriting it
questions.stem: A brief describes a civic hall's form as the product of the guilds that commissioned it, and treats the nineteenth-century roof as a later addition.

options.text: The guild structure shaped the hall for centuries, and the roof is one later layer
The roof determined the whole design, since it is the part visitors actually see
options.misconception: lets the most visible element stand for the whole structure

options.text: The guilds had no lasting effect, since the building has been rebuilt several times
options.misconception: erases a long-standing structure because of later interventions

options.text: The building's form follows no long structure at all, since architects design freely
options.misconception: assumes designers work without inherited constraints

questions.explanation: A long-duration structure is an arrangement that outlasts the generations who inherit it, and it keeps shaping later decisions. The brief replaces that persistence with attention to the most visible layer and a claim of free invention.
questions.hint: Ask which arrangement outlasted the people who built it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Level and rate over a long span
questions.learningObjective: Separate a slow long-run rate from concentrated change within it
questions.stem: A brief notes that a street's building height rose from three storeys to eight over four centuries, and treats the change as gradual improvement.

options.text: The change was gradual, so it shows no particular period mattered more than another
options.misconception: reads slow change as proof that no period stands out

options.text: The change was gradual, so the street never experienced a decisive moment
options.misconception: equates gradual change with the absence of turning points

options.text: The overall rate was slow, but two short periods could still dominate it
The change was gradual, so the street was never under pressure to build higher
options.misconception: reads slow change as an absence of pressure

questions.explanation: A slow long-run rate can contain short periods of very fast change, and the average is not the same as the history. The brief's emphasis on gradualness conceals the possibility that two decades did most of the work.
questions.hint: Ask which decades contributed most of the total rise.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Read adaptation inside a fixed frame as constraint in operation
questions.stem: A survey of a medieval town shows that the street widths stayed fixed for two centuries while the plot shapes changed repeatedly.

options.text: The plots changed freely, so the street width had no effect on them
options.misconception: treats change in one element as proof of no constraint from another

options.text: The fixed widths limited the plots, and the plots adapted within that limit
The plot changes prove the street widths changed as well, since both moved
options.misconception: claims co-movement without checking the direction

options.text: The street widths must have been ignored, since builders ignored them often
options.misconception: dismisses a constraint because it was sometimes breached

questions.explanation: A constraint that holds for two centuries while everything within it varies shows adaptation inside a limit rather than the absence of constraint. Plot shapes are the variable that absorbed the pressure, not evidence that the widths did nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what the fixed widths permitted and prevented.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to set common terms for comparing distant periods
questions.stem: Explain to a design team how two distant periods should be compared in a conservation brief.

answer.exemplar: Two distant periods should be compared on terms each can meet, which usually means comparing the same function and the same pressures rather than the same appearance. A brief that sets a roof of 1620 beside a roof of 1890 has to say what each was for, what each had to survive, and what each tells the survey about how the building was used and maintained. Only then can the differences be read as evidence of change, rather than as evidence that one period was simply better made. The comparison also has to name its own limits, since the earlier period left fewer records and those it left are usually about the parts that were repaired.

questions.explanation: Comparisons across distant periods need common terms of reference, and those terms are usually functional rather than visual. Without them, the comparison measures the survival of records instead of the life of the building.
questions.hint: Ask what each period can be compared on.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Specify the finding that would count against a structural claim

stimulus.body: A civic hall's plan is submitted for listing. The file argues that the building survives because its stone arcade was designed to carry a future upper storey that was never built. A surveyor's note in the same file records that three of the seven arcade piers were rebuilt in 1811 with thinner stones, and that the remaining four lean outward by two degrees.

questions.stem: Given this file, what would count against the argument about the arcade?

options.text: The file's argument is confirmed, since the unused upper floor proves the design was durable
options.misconception: treats a design intention as a record of the structure's state

options.text: The leaning and rebuilt piers could refute the claim about the arcades' strength
The file's argument stands, since a design for extra load makes the base stronger
options.misconception: reasons from an intention to a strength that was never tested

options.text: The surveyor is wrong, because leaning piers are normal in surviving arcades
options.misconception: normalises the very feature that would need explaining

questions.explanation: A disconfirmation is designed in advance by asking what finding would count against the claim. Here the leaning and replaced piers are exactly that, so the file should state in advance how such a finding would be treated.
questions.hint: Ask what finding would count against the claim.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Classify a change against the longer movement around it
questions.stem: A brief must classify a change in a workshop's roof span; which framing best handles the turning point question?

options.text: The span widened steadily for a century, so a few sharp years may not change the account
A sharp change in roof span is always the turning point of a building's history
options.misconception: assumes a visible change marks a turning point by itself

options.text: Only a change in ownership counts as a turning point in a building's history
options.misconception: fixes the measure of turning points on one type of change

options.text: Turning points are unknowable, so the brief should avoid classifying the change
options.misconception: treats a hard judgment as a reason to skip it

questions.explanation: A turning point has to be argued from how much of the later pattern the change explains, and a slow century-long trend may absorb several sharp episodes. Classifying it is necessary; refusing to classify it is not a finding.
questions.hint: Ask how much of the later pattern the change explains.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Order the steps required before explaining an absence
questions.stem: A brief asks why no medieval stone bridge survives in the valley, and the usual answer is that none was ever built.

options.text: The bridges were built and lost, and no written record survives to prove it
options.misconception: invents unrecorded construction to answer a gap

options.text: The valley was too poor to build bridges, so the absence proves the poverty
options.misconception: treats an absence as confirming a single assumed cause

options.text: Stone bridges of that era cannot survive, so nothing was ever built here
options.misconception: generalises from other regions without local evidence

options.text: An absence of surviving evidence needs a survey before causes are ranked

questions.explanation: Explaining a non-occurrence begins by establishing what would have been detectable, since absence of evidence and evidence of absence are different things. A survey of what survives and what the ground shows can then support or rule out the proposed causes.
questions.hint: Ask what a survey could still find in the valley.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Rank causes without letting proximity to the failure decide
questions.stem: A brief explains a fire that gutted a mill by naming the spark from a locomotive, and passes over the loose thatch that had been repaired for decades.

options.text: The spark caused the fire, since a spark is what a fire begins with
options.misconception: ranks causes by proximity to the ignition moment

options.text: The thatch caused the fire, since combustible material is the real danger
options.misconception: ranks causes by a general property of the material

options.text: The spark and the fuel load both explain the fire's scale
The cause cannot be ranked, since a fire always has several simultaneous causes
options.misconception: treats multiplicity as a reason to refuse comparison

questions.explanation: Immediacy is one criterion among several, and the scale of a fire usually turns on the fuel available as well as the ignition. The brief uses proximity to the moment of ignition as if it settled the whole explanation.
questions.hint: Ask what made the fire able to spread so far.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Read a dated sequence as a chain of enabling steps
questions.stem: A record shows that after a new drain was laid, the cellars dried, then the lime kilns were relit, and only then did the district's output rise.

options.text: The drain caused the output rise, since it came first in the sequence
options.misconception: credits the first link with the whole outcome

options.text: Each step made the next possible, so the chain carries the output rise
The relighting of the kilns caused the output rise, since it was closest to it
options.misconception: credits the nearest link instead of the whole chain

options.text: The four events are unrelated, since the record lists them together
options.misconception: reads co-occurrence in a record as independence

questions.explanation: The order and the dependency are what make this a chain: the drain enabled the kilns, and the kilns enabled the output. Credit for the outcome has to be spread across the steps that made it possible.
questions.hint: Ask which step made the next one possible.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a thesis across periods is built and tested
questions.stem: Explain to a conservation team how a thesis should be built across a long sequence of periods.

answer.exemplar: A thesis across periods needs an argument that the periods jointly support, which means stating what the sequence shows as a whole and then showing how each period contributes to it. A team working on a mill might claim that the building's repeated rebuilding tracks changes in the water power rather than changes in taste, and each phase then has to be checked for whether it fits that claim. The discipline lies in naming the period that fits least well, because a thesis that cannot be strained is not a thesis but a summary. The claim also has to survive the question of what would have been built if the events had not happened.

questions.explanation: A thesis is a claim about the whole sequence, and its strength comes from what each period contributes to it. Building it requires naming the weakest fit rather than only the confirming cases.
questions.hint: Ask which period fits the thesis least well.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a persistent framework from a renewed fabric

stimulus.body: A town's main street keeps the same alignment, the same plot widths and the same market rights from the thirteenth century to the present, although every building on it has been replaced at least once. The assessment notes that the street was repeatedly rebuilt in brick after fires, and that the market rights were confirmed in writing four times across the period.

questions.stem: Given this assessment, which description of the street fits best?

options.text: The street is unchanged, since its alignment has never moved
options.misconception: equates one preserved feature with an unchanged whole

options.text: The street is entirely new, since every building on it has been replaced
options.misconception: equates total rebuilding with the absence of continuity

options.text: The alignment alone proves the whole street's continuity
options.misconception: inflates a single retained feature into a complete account

options.text: A long-duration framework persisted while its parts were replaced

questions.explanation: Structures that outlast many generations often survive as frameworks of alignment, rights and plot sizes while their fabric is repeatedly renewed. That combination of persistent form and replaced parts is exactly what the record describes.
questions.hint: Ask what stayed fixed while the fabric was renewed.

questions.topic: Level and rate over a long span
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a level from a rate in a long-span series
questions.stem: A brief describes a city's growth; which statement best distinguishes its level from its rate?

options.text: The city's size shows the level, while growth per decade shows the rate
The level and the rate are the same figure expressed in different units
options.misconception: treats two different quantities as one measurement

options.text: Only the rate matters, since the level is simply the rate summed
options.misconception: dismisses a quantity as if it were derived from the other

options.text: The rate can only be measured over a single year to be meaningful
options.misconception: fixes an arbitrary measurement window on the quantity

questions.explanation: Level is how much there is and rate is how fast it is changing, and the two move independently over a long span. Keeping them apart stops a stable total being read as an absence of change.
questions.hint: Ask what each figure answers about the city.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Locate a designer's choice inside the conditions already fixed
questions.stem: A brief credits a nineteenth-century architect with the freedom of the site, though the plot, the street line and the client were all fixed beforehand.

options.text: The architect's genius explains the result, since the constraints were ordinary
options.misconception: credits personal talent while ignoring the fixed conditions

options.text: The constraints explain the result, so the architect's role was negligible
options.misconception: erases agency by turning constraints into the whole account

options.text: The architect's choices worked inside conditions that were already set
Constraints and choices are opposites, so only one of them can explain a design
options.misconception: frames agency and constraint as mutually exclusive

questions.explanation: Agency operates within constraints rather than against them, and both belong in the account of a finished design. Naming the fixed conditions shows what the designer was actually able to decide.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Require a common purpose before reading differences between periods
questions.stem: A brief compares a building of 1340 with the same building as rebuilt in 1820, focusing on the differences in window openings.

options.text: The window differences prove the earlier building was of a lower standard
options.misconception: ranks periods on a single presentational feature

options.text: The comparison needs a common purpose before the differences can be read
The two buildings cannot be compared, since they are four centuries apart
options.misconception: treats a long gap as an automatic bar on comparison

options.text: The later rebuilding is the better comparison, since more evidence survives
options.misconception: prefers the better documented period without argument

questions.explanation: Comparing across periods requires fixing what the two are being compared for, since a window can change for many reasons. The gap in time is not itself a barrier; an absent common purpose is.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the measurement a claim would have to predict
questions.stem: A brief argues that a stone vault survived because of its shallow rise; the vault's own geometry shows a rise of 1.4 metres over a 9 metre span.

options.text: The shallow rise supports the argument, since it keeps the vault low
options.misconception: treats a low measurement as confirming a claim about strength

options.text: The argument is refuted, since a shallow rise is structurally impossible
options.misconception: refutes a claim on a rule that was never tested

options.text: The rise figure is unimportant, since strength does not depend on geometry
options.misconception: dismisses the very measurement the claim would be tested against

options.text: A predicted rise from the claim would have been a sharper disconfirmation

questions.explanation: A well-designed disconfirmation states in advance what measurement would count against the claim. Here the brief records no expected figure, so the reading available cannot be used as the test the argument requires.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how absence of evidence differs from evidence of absence
questions.stem: Explain to a research team how the absence of surviving evidence should be handled in a brief.

answer.exemplar: An absence of evidence and evidence of absence are different things, and a brief that treats them as one will build its account on a gap. The first question is what would have survived if it had been made, since a timber building in a wet valley might leave no trace while a stone one would leave foundations, and that difference decides how much the absence can tell us. The second is whether other traces exist, in the ground, in the records or in later descriptions, which can turn an apparent absence into a demonstrated one. Only after that should the causes be ranked.

questions.explanation: Explaining a non-occurrence requires first establishing what was detectable and what remains to be found. Ranking causes before that step assigns blame to a gap in the record rather than to the past.
questions.hint: Ask what would have survived if the thing had existed.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Classify a change against the earlier pattern it sits inside

stimulus.body: A report on a mill describes a decisive change: in 1761 the mill wheel was replaced with a water frame, and within a decade the building's whole silhouette changed, with a taller house added at the weir end. The report also records that the wheel had been rebuilt twice before 1761, in 1712 and 1748, each time larger than the last, and that the sill level had been raised in 1740.

questions.stem: Given this report, how should the 1761 change be classified?

options.text: It was the turning point, because the silhouette changed so quickly afterwards
options.misconception: reads a rapid change in appearance as a decisive break

options.text: It was an ordinary rebuild, because wheels were replaced repeatedly at this mill
options.misconception: lets the prior pattern cancel the change in the record

options.text: It was a turning point within a rising trend that had begun decades earlier
It cannot be classified, because turning points are not observable in buildings
options.misconception: declares the judgment impossible instead of arguing it

questions.explanation: The report supports both facts: the wheel grew through earlier rebuilds, and 1761 produced a change of a different order. Calling 1761 a turning point within a longer rise keeps both rather than choosing one and discarding the other.
questions.hint: Ask what had been changing before 1761.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Frame choice and fixed conditions in the same account
questions.stem: A brief must explain a landlord's rebuild of a tenement; which framing best handles choice and condition?

options.text: The rebuild was forced by the landlord, so his decisions explain nothing
options.misconception: removes agency entirely once conditions are named

options.text: The rebuild was the landlord's choice, so the site's conditions are irrelevant
options.misconception: credits personal agency while ignoring fixed conditions

options.text: Neither the landlord nor the site explains the rebuild, since rebuilds are routine
options.misconception: dismisses both levels because the outcome looks ordinary

options.text: The landlord chose within conditions that limited what he could build

questions.explanation: Choice within constraint explains both the freedom and the limits of a decision, and each of the alternatives keeps one and drops the other. Naming the conditions is what makes the landlord's choices intelligible as choices.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Place an omitted factor inside a chain rather than outside it
questions.stem: A brief argues that a new sewer made a district's land more valuable, without mentioning that the district was also rezoned for housing.

options.text: The sewer caused the rise, since it is the only structure named
options.misconception: credits the only named intervention by default

options.text: The chain runs from sewer to housing to land value, and the rezoning belongs in it
The rezoning caused the rise, since planning decisions always dominate
options.misconception: reasons from a general expectation instead of the sequence

options.text: The rise came from wider market movements, so neither local change mattered
options.misconception: dismisses both local changes for an unexamined general cause

questions.explanation: The sewer would have had to act on land value through some route, and the rezoning is a plausible link in that route. A chain makes the mechanism visible and lets each step be tested.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Rank interacting causes rather than the one nearest the failure
questions.stem: A brief explains a roof collapse by naming the overloaded beam, and passes over the blocked gutter that had been overflowing all winter.

options.text: The overloaded beam caused the collapse, since it is where the failure appeared
options.misconception: ranks causes by where the failure was visible

options.text: The blocked gutter caused the collapse, since water damage is the real mechanism
options.misconception: ranks by mechanism without dating the events

options.text: The gutter load and the beam strength act on each other in sequence
The cause cannot be determined without a full structural inspection
options.misconception: declines to reason at all from the evidence already given

The two surveys show different buildings, so comparison is impossible
options.misconception: treats renewal of parts as the end of the building

options.misconception: inflates one retained measurement into complete survival

options.misconception: counts renewals as separate buildings without evidence

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a spanning thesis is assigned and tested
questions.stem: Explain to a planning team how to build a thesis across several periods of a building's history.

answer.exemplar: A thesis across periods states what the whole sequence shows and then assigns each period a job in supporting it. Working on a civic building, a team might claim that each rebuilding responded to a change in public practice, and then has to show for each phase what the practice was and what the rebuild addressed. A thesis is tested by naming the phase that fits worst and asking whether it can be read as an exception with a reason, or whether it undermines the claim. It is also tested by asking what would have been built if the triggering change had not occurred, since a thesis that explains everything after the fact explains nothing.

questions.explanation: A thesis across periods gives each phase a role and is tested against the phase that fits worst. Without that test the thesis becomes a summary of whatever happened to be built.
questions.hint: Ask which period the thesis handles worst.

options.misconception: picks the most visible feature rather than the longest-lived

options.text: The plot framework, which outlasted every change to the frontages
The family names, since they are the only continuous record in the file

options.text: The guild regulations, since they are the oldest document quoted
options.misconception: treats the age of a document as the age of what it describes

questions.explanation: The plot widths, the plot lines and the family tenure formed a framework that persisted for centuries while the visible fabric was repeatedly renewed. The survey lets the short-lived and long-lived features be told apart.

questions.learningObjective: Describe the freedom a designer actually had
questions.stem: Explain to a survey team how to describe the freedom a designer actually had.

answer.exemplar: Freedom in a design is bounded by what was settled in advance, by what the client could refuse, by the cost of materials and by the codes in force, and describing it means naming those bounds rather than implying a free hand. A brief that praises a builder's ingenuity without stating what was fixed cannot tell a reader how remarkable the choice was. Conversely, a brief that lists only the constraints reads the finished building as wholly determined, which erases the choices that were genuinely open. The two descriptions belong together: the fixed conditions and the decisions taken inside them.

questions.explanation: Freedom is only meaningful relative to what was fixed, so a brief should name the constraints and the choices together. Either alone produces a misleading account of how a building came to be.
questions.hint: Ask what was already settled when the decision was made.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Assess a comparative conclusion against the two records behind it

stimulus.body: A comparative report examines a city hall in 1720 and the same hall in 1920. The 1720 survey lists a single room used for the assizes, market and council meetings in turn. The 1920 report describes separate council and court chambers and records that the roof was raised to take a gallery. The report's conclusion states that the building had grown to match the institutions it housed.

questions.stem: Given this report, what supports the conclusion it draws?

options.text: The 1720 survey describes a single room, so nothing was really built
options.misconception: reads the earlier survey as denying any later building

options.text: The gallery was added for show, since the report mentions no other reason
options.misconception: supplies a motive the report never states

options.text: The separate rooms and the raised roof track the divided functions of 1920
The conclusion is unsupported, because two surveys cannot be compared
options.misconception: denies a comparison the report actually makes

questions.explanation: The two records describe the same building doing different jobs, and the physical changes correspond to the functional changes. That correspondence is what supports a conclusion about the building responding to its institutions.
questions.hint: Ask what the 1920 physical changes match in the 1920 functions.

questions.learningObjective: Describe a propagated change as an enabling sequence

options.text: Each change made the next possible, so the chain is the explanation
The first change was the cause, and the later ones were merely effects
options.misconception: compresses a chain into its first link

options.text: The changes were independent, since the record lists them separately
options.misconception: reads separate entries as separate causes

options.text: The chain is unnecessary, since the outcome is what needs explaining
options.misconception: treats the outcome as a substitute for a mechanism

questions.explanation: A chain explains how one change propagated, and each link is a candidate point of intervention. The alternatives either stop at the first link or treat separate records as separate causes.
questions.hint: Ask what each change made possible for the next.

questions.learningObjective: Read load and capacity together rather than ranking by timing

options.misconception: ranks causes by the moment of visible failure

options.text: The thinner columns caused the collapse, since capacity was reduced
options.misconception: ranks by capacity without reference to the load that acted

options.text: The changed columns and the added load have to be read together
The cause is undecidable, since both factors are physically relevant
options.misconception: refuses comparison because both candidates are real

options.misconception: treats placement rather than testability as the requirement

options.text: The thesis should claim something the periods can confirm or undermine

options.text: The thesis should avoid naming periods, since naming them invites dispute
options.misconception: seeks safety by refusing to be specific

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the durable layer within a repeatedly renewed building
questions.stem: A structural survey records that a hall's roof frame, floor joists and window openings all date from 1550, while the glass, plaster and flagstones have been replaced repeatedly since.

options.text: The hall is essentially unchanged, since its frame and openings survive
options.misconception: inflates surviving structure into complete preservation

options.text: The hall is entirely a modern building, since the surfaces are recent
options.misconception: lets recent surfaces erase the surviving frame

options.text: The hall's continuity lies in its materials, since stone always outlasts wood
options.misconception: reasons from a general material hierarchy

options.text: The structural frame is the long-duration element within a renewed fabric

questions.explanation: Buildings carry a hierarchy of durability, and the elements that last longest are often those least visible. Identifying which layer is the long-duration one is what lets change and continuity be described together.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to specify a disconfirmation in advance
questions.stem: Explain to a structural engineer how to design a disconfirmation for a claim about an old building.

answer.exemplar: A disconfirmation is designed by writing down, in advance, the observation that would count against the claim, and then making sure that observation is actually obtainable. A team claiming that a building survives because of its stone vaults might name the discovery of extensive timber repairs, or the collapse of comparable vaults, or a fall in the ground level under the building, and each of those is a possible finding rather than an argument. The design also has to address what would be found if the search came up empty, since a disconfirmation that cannot return a negative result is not a test. Recording the expected result before the work is the difference between a test and a confirmation.

questions.explanation: A disconfirmation states in advance what would count against the claim, so that a finding can actually be unwelcome. Without that specification, the investigation can only confirm what it began with.
questions.hint: Ask what finding would count against the claim.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Classify a step change inside a long slow movement

stimulus.body: A town's grain market records the arrival of a new weighbridge in 1811, after which the recorded tonnage rises from about 400 quarters a year to about 900 within a decade. The record also notes that the tonnage had risen from 300 to 380 over the previous two centuries, and that a second weighbridge was built at the inland market in 1830.

questions.stem: Given this record, which reading is best supported?

options.text: The weighbridge did nothing, since tonnage was already rising before 1811
options.misconception: treats a prior slow rise as cancelling a later step change

options.text: The tonnage rise was simply a continuation of the earlier slow trend
options.misconception: assumes continuity where the record shows a step

options.text: The 1811 weighbridge is the only possible cause, since it is the only dated change
options.misconception: credits the only named intervention by default

options.text: A long slow rise was followed by a step change in the early nineteenth century

questions.explanation: The record contains both a gradual rise over two centuries and a much faster change after 1811, and the classification must keep both. Calling the whole period a continuation, or crediting the weighbridge for everything, discards one of the two facts.
questions.hint: Ask how the tonnage changed before and after 1811.

options.misconception: credits the earlier link with the whole outcome

options.text: The style change caused the route change, since styles are easier to date
options.misconception: reverses a sequence on the basis of dating convenience

Neither change caused the other, since they belong to different fields
options.misconception: seeks an explanation in disciplinary separation

The similarities show the building was preserved exactly as it was first built
options.misconception: treats appearance as a complete record of the building

options.text: The comparison is unneeded, since a single building speaks for its whole history
options.misconception: relies on one object instead of comparing records

options.text: The differences should be ignored, since they show the later period was worse
options.misconception: discards evidence on grounds of judgement rather than relevance

questions.explanation: Comparison across periods gains from asking which aspects of the object are being held constant and which are not. A visual similarity says little about use, ownership or internal arrangement, all of which usually change over three centuries.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Refuse a single survivor as an explanation for a regional absence
questions.stem: A brief notes that no grand stair survives in the county's houses, and explains it by the presence of a ladder stair in one surviving house.

options.text: The ladder stair explains the absence, since it shows what was normal
options.misconception: generalises from one survivor to a whole county

options.text: One survivor cannot explain an absence across the county
The absence cannot be explained, since no county ever had grand stairs
options.misconception: infers an absence of the thing itself from an absence of the thing

options.text: The brief should simply omit the staircase, since it is a minor detail
options.misconception: removes awkward evidence instead of dealing with it

questions.explanation: A single survivor shows that the feature existed, not that it was typical, and it cannot by itself account for an absence elsewhere. Explaining a non-occurrence requires evidence about how widespread the practice was, not one example of it.

questions.learningObjective: Locate choice inside fixed plot widths
questions.stem: In a survey of a medieval town, sixteen of twenty-two surviving houses stand on plots of less than six metres width, and the plots cannot be widened because neighbours hold them.

options.text: House builders chose narrow plots freely, since nothing prevented wider choices
options.misconception: assumes free choice where the record shows none

options.text: Narrow plots caused the houses, and the builders had no part in them
options.misconception: removes the maker from the account entirely

options.text: The plot widths reflect a shortage of land, so the houses follow from scarcity
options.misconception: asserts a single cause for the widths without local evidence

options.text: The builders worked within fixed plot widths, and the choice lay in the rest

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the test that separates a turning point from a trend
questions.stem: Explain to a heritage officer how to decide whether a change is a turning point or part of a long trend.

answer.exemplar: The decision turns on how much of the later pattern the change explains, and the test is comparative rather than impressionistic. If a change of 1811 is followed by two centuries of the new level, it is a turning point; if the new level then drifts on for the same trajectory as before, it is part of the trend. The distinction matters because the two support different stories, one about a break and one about persistence, and they also imply different points for intervention or conservation. A team should state which test it applied and which period of the record it used, since the classification can shift as evidence extends.

questions.explanation: A turning point earns the name by explaining the subsequent pattern, and that is a comparative test rather than a judgement about drama. Saying which test and which span were used keeps the classification open to revision.
questions.hint: Ask how much of the later pattern the change explains.

questions.topic: Level and rate over a long span
questions.learningObjective: Read divergent level and rate across two series

stimulus.body: A city archive records its population at 12000 in 1500, 40000 in 1700, 90000 in 1900 and 95000 in 1950, and notes that the four surrounding villages together held 30000 residents in 1950 against 20000 in 1900. The archivist observes that the city stopped growing quickly around the middle of the nineteenth century while the region as a whole continued to grow.

questions.stem: Given these figures, what does the record show about level and rate?

options.text: The city and the region both grew steadily at the same rate throughout
options.misconception: smooths distinct series into a single rate

options.text: The region shrank, since the city's increase exceeded the region's
options.misconception: misreads the arithmetic of the two figures

options.text: The city settled at a plateau while the region around it grew
Population figures cannot describe a rate without annual records
options.misconception: demands daily resolution for a multi-century rate

questions.explanation: A stable city total and a rising regional total are both visible in the figures, and the level and the rate have clearly diverged. The record's comment that the city plateaued matches the numbers rather than replacing them.
questions.hint: Ask which series settled and which kept rising.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to write an account of choice within fixed conditions
questions.stem: Explain to a heritage team how to write an account of design choice within fixed conditions.

answer.exemplar: An account of design choice begins with the conditions that were not open, such as the site, the client, the budget and the codes, and then describes what was decided inside them. This ordering matters because it converts praise or blame into something checkable: a decision that was genuinely open can be assessed, and one that was fixed cannot be praised as if it were a choice. It also stops the account from sliding into either pure determinism, in which nothing was decided, or pure genius, in which everything was. The fixed conditions are usually recoverable from the record, since contracts, leases and permits state them, and the brief can point to them rather than assert them.

questions.explanation: Agency is legible only against the conditions that were fixed, and both are recoverable from the record. Writing them in that order turns an assessment of a designer into something a reader can check.
questions.hint: Ask which conditions the record shows were already fixed.

questions.learningObjective: Weigh an exception against the pattern it interrupts

The report notes that in the second phase the wheel was enlarged while the leat was shortened, which it treats as an exception that does not alter the pattern.

options.misconception: lets a single exception dissolve a thesis without weighing it

options.text: The thesis is supported by the pattern and weakened by the one exception

options.misconception: treats admitting a weakness as removing it

options.text: The report should drop the second phase, since the thesis reads better without it
options.misconception: proposes removing inconvenient evidence

questions.explanation: A thesis is tested by the period that fits worst, and here three of four phases support the pattern while one does not. The correct response is to weigh the exception against the pattern rather than to suppress either.
questions.hint: Ask what the second phase does to the pattern.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to build a testable causal chain
questions.stem: Explain to a records office how to build a causal chain from a sequence of recorded changes.

answer.exemplar: A chain is built by identifying each step and, crucially, the link between consecutive steps, since a list of events is not yet a chain. The team asks what each change made possible for the next, and rejects any step that does not connect to its neighbour in a way the record supports. The test of the finished chain is that it predicts the timing and the size of the final outcome, so that the account can fail. It is also worth asking whether the order could have been reversed, because a chain that only works in one direction is often a chronology with extra confidence. Finally, a chain is the right form when no single step is sufficient, which is exactly the case a one-cause account cannot express.

questions.explanation: A chain is distinguished from a chronology by the links between steps, and its strength is that it can be tested against timing and size. A list of changes in order cannot fail, and so explains nothing in particular.
questions.hint: Ask what each step made possible for the next.

options.misconception: counts supporting phases without regard to what was omitted

options.text: The thesis must be dropped, since one phase is missing from the evidence
options.misconception: treats an evidentiary gap as a refutation

options.text: The thesis should be narrowed to the three phases that are documented
options.misconception: restricts a claim to the evidence rather than testing it

options.text: The omitted phase must be examined, because a thesis must face its worst case

questions.explanation: A thesis is tested against the phase that fits worst, and skipping that phase leaves the claim untested rather than safe. The obligation is to examine the omitted phase, not to narrow the claim around it.
questions.hint: Ask what the omitted phase would show.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Measure a bounded freedom against the conditions that bound it
questions.stem: A brief praises a builder for the freedom of a courtyard plan, though the plot was enclosed on three sides and the fourth was a party wall.

options.text: The builder's freedom is clear, since the plan shows great originality
options.misconception: reads apparent originality as actual freedom

options.text: The freedom was real but narrow, set by three sides and a wall
A courtyard plan shows the site was unconstrained, since such plans are open
options.misconception: assumes a form of plan indicates an open site

options.text: There was no freedom at all, since a party wall fixes everything
options.misconception: converts a bounded choice into a total absence of choice

questions.explanation: A plan that looks bold can still have been tightly bounded, and the fixed sides and party wall are the conditions that made the choice narrow. Naming those bounds is what makes the builder's achievement assessable.
questions.hint: Ask what the site fixed before the plan was drawn.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Read persistence of structure against change of use
questions.stem: A survey of a market hall in 1650 lists six market stalls, and a survey of the same hall in 1950 lists eleven, with the original stone frame still in place.

options.text: The frame proves the hall was never altered between the two dates
options.misconception: infers complete preservation from a surviving frame

options.text: The two surveys show different buildings, so no comparison is possible
options.misconception: denies a comparison that the shared frame makes possible

options.text: The frame persisted while the use inside it changed
The increase in stalls proves the market grew because of the frame
options.misconception: credits a surviving structure with a change in activity

questions.explanation: The two records describe one structure with different use inside it, and that pairing is exactly what makes the comparison informative. A surviving frame says nothing about whether the hall was otherwise the same.
questions.hint: Ask what changed inside the frame.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to write an account of something that did not happen
questions.stem: Explain to a review panel how to write an explanation for something that did not happen.

answer.exemplar: An explanation for a non-occurrence begins with what the evidence could have shown, because the gap may be in the record rather than in the past. The team asks what a surviving instance would have left behind, such as foundations, fragments, a name in a document or a reference in a later description, and then checks which of those traces are still available. Only after that can causes be ranked, and the ranking will distinguish causes that prevented the thing, causes that made it invisible to later observers, and causes that made it hard to record in the first place. Those three are different claims and call for different remedies.

questions.explanation: Explaining a non-occurrence requires establishing what was detectable before ranking causes at all. Causes that prevented the thing, causes that hid it from later observers, and causes that made it unrecordable are different claims.
questions.hint: Ask what a surviving instance would have left behind.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Weigh a stated exception against a spanning thesis

stimulus.body: A heritage study follows a market hall from 1600 to 1900 and concludes that the hall's repeated enlargements tracked the growth of the town's market trade. The study sets out four enlargements and dates them to 1604, 1668, 1741 and 1830. It notes that the largest enlargement, in 1741, was ordered after a fire destroyed much of the hall, and it argues that this one was a rebuild rather than a response to trade.

questions.stem: Given this heritage study, how should the stated thesis be handled?

options.text: The thesis is proved, because four enlargements support it
options.misconception: counts supporting instances as if they settled the question

options.text: The thesis fails, because one enlargement had a different cause
options.misconception: lets one exception dissolve a well-supported pattern

options.text: The 1741 fire is irrelevant, since the hall was rebuilt to a larger size
options.misconception: treats the motive of a rebuild as without consequence

options.text: The thesis holds for three phases and needs the fire case accounted for

questions.explanation: A thesis is tested by its worst-fitting phase, and the study itself sets out the exception and argues around it. The defensible position is that the pattern holds where the causes differ and that the fire case needs to be stated in the thesis rather than left out of it.
questions.hint: Ask what the 1741 enlargement does to the pattern.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: State what makes a sequence explanatory rather than chronological
questions.stem: A brief must show how a series of recorded changes produced a final outcome; which statement is right?

options.text: Each step made the next possible, and the chain predicts the outcome's timing
The first recorded change caused the outcome, since it came earliest
options.misconception: credits the earliest link with the whole chain

options.text: The changes are a chronology, and a chronology explains outcomes by listing them
options.misconception: mistakes an ordered list for an explanatory mechanism

options.text: The outcome needs no mechanism, since it is the fact that requires explaining
options.misconception: treats the thing to be explained as its own explanation

questions.explanation: A chain is explanatory rather than chronological because each link enables the next and the finished chain can be tested against timing and size. The alternatives stop at the first link or abandon the mechanism altogether.
questions.hint: Ask what each change made possible for the next.
